title: Given a number N, generate all structurally unique binary search trees that store values 1 through N. Explain how choosing each value as the root and recursively building left and right subtrees enumerates every shape.
shortTitle: Structurally Unique Binary Search Trees (Generate All Shapes)

s1_definition.profdef: Structurally Unique Binary Search Trees is a Subsets-pattern divide-and-conquer problem. For values in a range, we pick each value in turn as the root; all smaller values form the left subtree and all larger values form the right subtree. We recursively generate every left-subtree shape and every right-subtree shape, then pair each left shape with each right shape under the chosen root. The count of trees is the Catalan number, and each is a distinct BST.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, an interest-tier lookup can be organized as a search tree over tier numbers one to N, and different tree shapes give different lookup performance. The analytics team wants every valid tree shape to benchmark. We pick each tier as the root, put the lower tiers on the left and the higher tiers on the right, build every shape of each side, and combine them.
s1_definition.oneliner: Make each value the root, recurse to build all left and all right subtree shapes, and pair them under the root.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Structurally Unique Binary Search Trees is a Subsets-pattern divide-and-conquer problem. For values in a range, we pick each value in turn as the root; all smaller values form the left subtree and all larger values form the right subtree. We recursively generate every left-subtree shape and every right-subtree shape, then pair each left shape with each right shape under the chosen root. The count of trees is the Catalan number, and each is a distinct BST.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, an interest-tier lookup can be organized as a search tree over tier numbers one to N, and different tree shapes give different lookup performance. The analytics team wants every valid tree shape to benchmark. We pick each tier as the root, put the lower tiers on the left and the higher tiers on the right, build every shape of each side, and combine them.

**One line to remember:** Make each value the root, recurse to build all left and all right subtree shapes, and pair them under the root.

sections.s2_technical:
We define a recursion over an inclusive range, `generate(start, end)`, returning a list of all tree roots for that range. If `start > end` the range is empty and we return a single-element list containing `null`, which represents a missing subtree and is essential for pairing. For each value i from start to end we recursively generate `leftTrees = generate(start, i - 1)` and `rightTrees = generate(i + 1, end)`.

Then we pair: for each left-subtree root and each right-subtree root we create a new node with value i, attach the two subtrees, and add it to the result. For example, `TreeNode root = new TreeNode(i); root.left = l; root.right = r; result.add(root);`. Memoizing by range can avoid recomputation when only counting, though generating distinct node objects typically rebuilds them.

A senior-level nuance is the empty-range sentinel: returning a list with one null lets the pairing loops run once even when a subtree is absent, which is what correctly produces trees where the root has only one child. Another nuance is that the number of shapes is the Catalan number, so N must be small for generation.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores interest tiers one to N in a binary search tree for lookups, and because tree shape affects lookup depth, analytics wants to enumerate every valid shape to benchmark lookup performance. This is exactly how Structurally Unique BSTs works: each shape is one arrangement with the BST ordering preserved.

Problem 2 — Hand-drawing tree shapes is incomplete beyond the tiniest N. This is why we generate them recursively, choosing each tier as the root and combining all left and right shapes, which guarantees completeness.

The code defines a `TierNode` and a `BstShapesService` exposing `allShapes(n)` returning the list of tree roots, plus a helper to render a tree as a parenthesized string for logging. A `Demo` runs it for N equal to three and logs the five shapes.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: N equal to three, so tiers are 1, 2, 3.

Step 1: Choose root 1. The left range is empty, returning a null sentinel; the right range is 2 to 3, which itself has two shapes, 2 with right child 3, and 3 with left child 2. Pairing gives two trees rooted at 1.

Step 2: Choose root 2. The left range is just 1, one shape; the right range is just 3, one shape. Pairing gives one balanced tree rooted at 2 with children 1 and 3.

Step 3: Choose root 3. The left range is 1 to 2, which has two shapes, 1 with right child 2, and 2 with left child 1; the right range is empty. Pairing gives two trees rooted at 3.

Step 4: The total is two plus one plus two equal to five shapes, which is the third Catalan number.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  tiers 1..3, pick each as root
    │
    ├ root 1: left=empty, right=generate(2,3)=2 shapes → 2 trees
    ├ root 2: left=generate(1,1)=1, right=generate(3,3)=1 → 1 tree
    └ root 3: left=generate(1,2)=2 shapes, right=empty → 2 trees
    │
    ▼
  5 structurally unique BSTs (Catalan(3))
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Structurally Unique Binary Search Trees asks me to generate every distinct BST that stores the values one through N. I use divide and conquer driven by the BST ordering property. I pick each value in turn as the root; everything smaller must form the left subtree and everything larger the right subtree. I recursively generate every possible left-subtree shape and every possible right-subtree shape over those ranges, then pair each left shape with each right shape under the chosen root to form complete trees.

The detail that makes the recursion clean is the empty-range sentinel. When the range is empty I return a list containing a single null, which represents a missing subtree, so the pairing loops still execute once and correctly produce trees whose root has only one child. I also note that the number of shapes is the Catalan number, which grows quickly, so generation is only practical for small N.

At the National Bank of India I used this to benchmark interest-tier lookup trees, where tiers one to N were stored in a BST and the tree shape affected lookup depth, so analytics wanted every valid shape to measure. I generated the shapes by choosing each tier as root and combining all left and right sub-shapes, and rendered each tree in a parenthesized form for the benchmark report. Explaining how the BST ordering splits the range and why the empty-range sentinel is needed is what shows an interviewer that I can turn a structural property into a correct generative recursion.
